sentences.text: This large marine reptile exceeded ten meters in total length, with paddle-like limbs stretching nearly three meters.
One specific specimen from Antarctica suggests a size greater than eleven meters, while its estimated wingspan reached approximately seven meters.
The genus was established by Ángel Cabrera in 1941, based on a specimen from Chubut Province, Argentina.
The holotype, found in the Lefipán Formation, was donated to the Museo de La Plata in September 1940.
A second species, Aristonectes quiriquinensis, was described in 2014, following the initial discovery of a single tail bone on Quiriquina Island.
Its skull shape indicates it likely fed by mixing prey and sediment in deep-water zones.
It is hypothesized that the animal used gastroliths to aid digestion, though using them to reduce buoyancy is poorly supported.
Curved neck ribs and neural spines likely allowed the creature to keep its trunk higher than its head.
Recent studies classify the genus among the elasmosaurids.
These animals lived during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
Fossils have been recovered from what are now Patagonia and Antarctica, including a specimen from the López de Bertodano Formation.
Evidence suggests the animal regularly migrated between these two southern landmasses.
Researchers debate whether the original tail bone from Quiriquina Island belongs to Aristonectes parvidens.
It is likely that A. quiriquinensis possessed fewer teeth than A. parvidens, based on preserved tooth sockets.
In 1962, Samuel P. Welles considered the animal to be an indeterminate pliosaur due to its enigmatic anatomy.
O'Keefe and colleagues expressed skepticism in 2011 about grouping Aristonectes and Kaiwhekea with Tatenectes because of morphological differences.
